ABSTRACT
Ultrasound (US) imaging is widely used in image-­guided therapies due to its real-­time capability, high temporal resolution, cost-­
effectiveness, safety, and portability. While many US tracking methods exist, most reviews focus on conventional techniques and 
overlook recent advances in deep learning (DL). Existing DL surveys often emphasize modalities like MRI (Magnetic Resonance 
Imaging) or CT (Computed Tomography), but US tracking presents unique challenges, such as speckle noise, acoustic shadow-
ing, and occlusions, that require tailored solutions. With increasing interest in automating US-­guided procedures, particularly 
for respiratory-­induced motion (RIM) tracking, this review fills a gap by focusing on recent DL-­based methods specifically 
developed for US motion tracking. We conducted a targeted review of state-­of-­the-­art DL techniques, categorizing them by net-
work architecture. Special attention is given to studies using benchmark datasets like CLUST (Challenge on Liver Ultrasound 
Tracking), which enable standardized performance comparison. DL-­based methods demonstrate improved accuracy and robust-
ness in difficult scenarios, such as out-­of-­plane motion and occlusions, where traditional approaches often underperform. DL 
has significantly improved the feasibility of markerless US tracking in clinical settings, supporting more automated and reliable 
image-­guided interventions. While conventional methods still offer value, hybrid strategies that integrate DL with traditional 
tracking or sensor fusion approaches show strong potential. This review complements prior surveys on conventional US tracking, 
serving as a useful resource for researchers developing robust, automated US-­based applications.
1   |   Introduction
Respiratory-­induced motion (RIM) poses a significant challenge 
across a broad spectrum of medical imaging applications, in-
cluding image-­guided radiation therapy (IGRT), robotic-­assisted 
surgeries, diagnostic imaging, and image-­guided interventions 
[1, 2]. RIM can lead to image artifacts, reduced diagnostic ac-
curacy, misalignment with surrounding healthy tissues, and 
compromised therapeutic outcomes. To address these challenges, 
motion tracking has emerged as a critical technique. A wide range 
of tracking and prediction models, from linear filters to advanced 
deep learning (DL) algorithms, have been developed to estimate 
the position of moving targets [3, 4]. Leading technology manufac-
turers have introduced devices for RIM tracking, some of which 
are already in clinical use [5, 6]. These extensive studies highlight 
the importance of improving this technique to enhance precision,

CT (Computed Tomography) [7, 8], MRI (Magnetic Resonance 
Imaging) [4, 9], and x-­ray [10, 11] with limited studies focusing 
on ultrasound (US) imaging for tracking models. Despite this, 
US imaging offers unique advantages, including superior tem-
poral resolution for capturing dynamic organ movements, cost-­
effectiveness, real-­time imaging capabilities, safety, accessibility, 
and portability due to its compact and mobile design [12]. These 
features make it an increasingly popular choice for quantitative 
applications like detection, segmentation, tracking, and there is a 
growing push to integrate automation into US-­based treatments 
[12–14]. Additionally, challenges associated with current treat-
ments using other modalities have made US an appealing alterna-
tive, particularly for tasks such as tracking anatomical landmarks 
in image-­guided treatments. For example, a key challenge in cur-
rent image-­guided treatments is that modern linear accelerators 
(LINACs) are equipped with on-­board 3D cone beam computed 
tomography (CBCT) and 2D x-­ray imaging, both commonly used 
for patient setup during treatment. While 2D x-­ray fluoroscopy 
offers high temporal resolution, its poor soft tissue contrast often 
necessitates the use of implanted fiducial markers. Additionally, 
the radiation dose associated with x-­ray-­based imaging remains 
a concern in radiation therapy [15, 16]. Modalities such as MRI 
provide superior soft tissue contrast without ionizing radiation, 
addressing these limitations. However, MRI-­LINAC systems are 
expensive and lack real-­time volumetric imaging capabilities. To 
address these challenges, new medical devices are emerging, and 
there is a growing need to integrate automated tracking with US 
technology, especially since current US systems are capable of 2D, 
3D, and 4D imaging, and they can be used both in the planning 
and treatment stages of the treatment workflow.
US images are often difficult to interpret due to small acoustic 
windows and sensitivity to noise and artifacts, such as shad-
ows and mirroring caused by highly attenuating or reflective 
structures [17]. While some artifacts can aid diagnosis, they are 
unstable in dynamic tissues, complicating motion estimation. 
These limitations have led to the development of conventional 
tracking methods, including block-­matching-­based speckle 
tracking [18], feature-­based techniques [19], optical flow [20], 
and template matching [18]. However, these methods remain 
sensitive to common US shortcomings such as shadows, speckle 
noise, and gain variability. Comparative surveys further assess 
the techniques performance [17, 18, 21–23].
While conventional tracking approaches achieve impressive re-
sults, they often involve a significant trade-­off between perfor-
mance and run-­time. This limitation is especially evident when 
processing 4D data, where run-­times can extend to several seconds, 
making real-­time application challenging [24, 25]. DL has recently 
gained traction as a powerful tool for overcoming the limitations 
of conventional methods by providing end-­to-­end processing. It 
has particularly advanced the field of markerless tracking, mak-
ing it more accurate, robust, and feasible for clinical applications. 
Unlike traditional methods that rely on markers, markerless track-
ing uses DL to directly analyze US images and infer motion with-
out the need for additional hardware or manual intervention. This 
approach leverages the power of convolutional neural networks 
(CNNs) [26, 27], recurrent neural networks (RNNs) [28, 29], and 
other DL architectures to extract features, model motion patterns, 
and predict organ positions in real time. Markerless tracking is es-
pecially valuable in non-­invasive treatments, as it eliminates the 
risks and complexities associated with marker placement while 
maintaining high precision. With the growing adoption of DL, 
these techniques are increasingly being integrated into the opti-
mization components of tracking and registration methods, as re-
viewed in [30–32]. However, most are designed for MRI, CT, and 
x-­ray, while US tracking presents distinct challenges that require 
specialized approaches. To fully leverage DL advancements, it is 
crucial to explore their application in US tracking. Given the re-
cent push to automate US procedures [33, 34] reviewing the latest 
developments in this area is essential for driving further progress. 
While some recent reviews [35] have focused on US tracking in 
elastography, comprehensive reviews covering other applications 
such as RIM tracking for image-­guided treatments remain limited.
US imaging includes several modalities, each designed for differ-
ent clinical purposes. B-­mode (brightness mode) is the most com-
monly used, producing 2D grayscale images that represent tissue 
structures based on backscattered echo intensity. Doppler ultra-
sonography assesses motion, typically blood flow, by measuring 
frequency shifts due to the Doppler effect. M-­mode (motion mode) 
captures high-­temporal-­resolution movement along a single scan 
line, commonly used in cardiac imaging. Elastography estimates 
tissue stiffness by measuring strain or shear wave propagation, 
aiding in disease characterization. Among these, B-­mode imaging 
is particularly suited for large motion estimation due to its wide 
field of view, high frame rate, and clear anatomical contrast. This 
review focuses on B-­mode DL-­based tracking methods for RIM 
in 2D and 3D US, addressing challenges like out-­of-­plane motion, 
noise, and artifacts, while emphasizing safe, cost-­effective, and 
non-­invasive solutions for image-­guided treatments. Only studies 
validated on real tissue data are included, ensuring clinical rele-
vance. The review spans the past decade, particularly following the 
CLUST (Challenge on Liver Ultrasound Tracking) competition, to 
highlight recent methodological advancements in DL-­based US 
tracking. RIM in abdominal organs can involve displacements 
of up to 4–5 cm; therefore, we exclude elastography [35], as strain 
imaging and time-­delay methods focus on small-­scale mechanical 
displacements. Another review [36] considers respiratory motion 
but emphasizes clinical aspects rather than US-­based tracking.
This article is structured as follows. In Foundations of US 
Tracking, we discuss the challenges associated with 2D and 3D 
US imaging, the available datasets for each, and the commonly 
used performance metrics. In Section  3, we review DL-­based 
motion estimation strategies and evaluate their performance by 
comparing their performance, highlighting their strengths and 
limitations in the Discussion section. Finally, the Conclusion 
and Future Direction summarize the current state of research 
and outline potential future directions in the field.

2.1   |   2D, 3D, and 4D US
Tracking in 2D, 3D, and 4D US varies significantly in terms of 
motion representation, computational complexity, and clini-
cal applicability. In this paper, we follow standard convention 
where 2D US refers to planar imaging over time (2D + t), but the 
temporal aspect is often implied. 3D US refers to static volumet-
ric acquisitions, while 4D US explicitly denotes time-­resolved 3D 
volumes (3D + t). 2D US, while limited to in-­plane motion, offers 
the advantages of rapid acquisition and lower computational 
demands. In contrast, 3D US enables volumetric motion track-
ing by capturing data across all spatial dimensions, improving 
motion estimation accuracy. However, it introduces challenges 
related to lower frame rates, increased data storage and process-
ing requirements, and reduced spatial resolution due to slice 
reconstruction. Various 3D acquisition methods such as free-
hand sweeping, mechanical sweeping, and matrix array probes 
present trade-­offs between data consistency, acquisition speed, 
and field of view. 4D US, which incorporates the temporal di-
mension, enables real-­time volumetric motion tracking and is 
particularly suited for continuous monitoring. Nonetheless, its 
implementation requires substantial computational resources, 
often addressed through GPU acceleration, reduced-­resolution 
imaging, and deep learning-­based motion prediction. Hybrid 
approaches combining 2D and 3D imaging offer a practical 
compromise, balancing accuracy, speed, and computational ef-
ficiency for clinical use. In this review, we categorize methods 
under 2D and 3D US tracking. While 4D US refers to dynamic 
3D imaging over time (3D + t), current literature on dedicated 
4D tracking methods is limited. Many 3D tracking methods can 
be extended to 4D scenarios [37, 38], but achieving real-­time per-
formance remains a major challenge. Therefore, we discuss 4D 
tracking within the broader context of 3D tracking.
2.2   |   Performance Evaluation
A validation framework should assess and potentially quantify 
several factors, including precision, accuracy, robustness, reli-
ability, computational complexity, and clinical applicability of 
a specific tracking approach. For landmark tracking, accuracy 
is typically reported as the average deviation between the pre-
dicted or estimated location of tracked landmarks and their true 
positions (ground truth) as TE (tracking error). This difference 
is often quantified as the mean geometric (Euclidean) distance 
(MED) between the points. Common error measures include 
mean squared error (MSE), root mean square error (RMSE), and 
mean absolute difference (MAD), which are usually reported 
alongside the standard deviation (std) to indicate the consis-
tency of the method across different frames.
2.3   |   Datasets
The CLUST dataset [17, 18, 21] includes liver US sequences ac-
quired under free-­breathing conditions from both patients and 
healthy volunteers, contributed by six research groups. The se-
quences were captured using six different US scanners, seven 
types of transducers, and various acquisition settings. The full 
dataset comprises 64 2D sequences from 63 subjects and 22 3D 
sequences from 18 subjects, with durations ranging from 4 s to 
10 min and frame rates between 6 and 31 Hz.
The data were anonymized and for evaluation purposes, 24 
2D and 7 3D sequences were designated by the organizers as 
the training set, with annotations provided for approximately 
10%–13% of the frames. The test set includes 39 2D and 14 3D 
sequences, with annotations typically limited to the first frame. 
One additional sequence in each modality was provided outside 
the official evaluation set, bringing the total to 64 2D and 22 
3D sequences. Studies using this dataset typically trained their 
models on the annotated training set and evaluated perfor-
mance on the designated test set to ensure consistent and fair 
benchmarking.
All annotations were created by the challenge organizers and 
manually labeled by three experienced observers, with the 
final landmark positions computed as the average of their an-
notations to reduce individual bias. The reported inter-­observer 
variability is approximately 0.5–0.6 mm for 2D and 1.2–1.8 mm 
for 3D, providing a reference for the expected upper bound of 
accuracy. Reported tracking errors in the sub-­millimeter range 
should therefore be interpreted in light of this annotation uncer-
tainty. Example annotated frames are shown in Figure 1.
Another dataset, provided by Ipsen et  al. [33], includes five 
long-­term 3D US liver sequences acquired under robotic com-
pensation for breathing-­induced motion from different healthy 
volunteers. The US probe was mounted on a robotic arm, which 
applied a continuous force of 10 N to maintain consistent con-
tact with the subject's surface at a manually selected position. 
The images have a mean spatial resolution of 1.0 × 0.7 × 1.5 mm3 
(length × depth × width) and a mean size of 250 × 253 × 128 vox-
els. Each US sequence includes one landmark annotation for 
two 30-­s segments (in total, 10 sequence of 30 s). Examples of 
this dataset are shown in Figure 2 where three selected sequence 
was annotated by three experts, each labeling three landmarks 
in two 30-­s segments [39]. Recently, an observer variability 
study on this dataset was published [40], reporting mean intra-­
observer variability ranging from 1.58 ± 0.90 to 2.05 ± 1.22 mm, 
and inter-­observer variability of 2.68 ± 1.69 and 3.06 ± 1.74 mm 
for the two observer groups.

3.1   |   2D Ultrasound Tracking
2D US tracking estimates in-­plane motion using sequences of B-­
mode frames. These methods benefit from fast acquisition, high 
frame rates, and ease of integration into image-­guided therapy 
systems. However, they face challenges such as limited depth 
information and sensitivity to out-­of-­plane motion. DL models 
for 2D tracking typically focus on extracting spatial and tempo-
ral features from frame sequences. In this section, we group 2D 
models based on their network architecture.
3.1.1   |   CNNs
CNNs are a type of DL network that replaces general matrix 
multiplication with convolution operations. These operations 
use sliding filters to capture spatial patterns, making CNNs 
highly effective for visual and imagery signal processing by 
learning discriminative local features showing superior perfor-
mance compared to handcrafted features.
Nouri and Rothberg [41] proposed a CNN-­based method for 
landmark tracking in long 2D US sequences from the CLUST 
dataset. The network learned a distance metric to compare 
image patches in a low-­dimensional embedding space, enabling 
patch-­based tracking across frames. Tested on 24 US sequences 
with 62 annotated landmarks, the method achieved a mean 
tracking error of 2.83 ± 4.86 mm with a runtime of approx-
imately 200 ms per annotation per frame. While it was one of 
the first DL approaches for US tracking, the model was not fully 
convolutional, lacked temporal modeling, and exhibited high 
variance, especially when tracking failed. Another pioneering 
study [26] employed CNNs to estimate motion between consec-
utive US images by inputting image pairs and directly regress-
ing transformation parameters (e.g., translation and rotation). 
These foundational efforts in 2D US paved the way for more 
specialized DL methods targeting tasks such as RIM tracking.
The proposed US motion tracking method in [42] integrates 
multilevel temporal information and unified visual features to 
enhance tracking accuracy and efficiency (Figure 3). The pro-
cess begins with a Time Adaptive CNN (TACNN), which dy-
namically adjusts convolutional weights to capture temporal 
variations in 2D US sequences. To enhance temporal consis-
tency, a Time Knowledge Accumulation (TKA) block is intro-
duced, capturing dependencies between frames. Additionally, a 
parallel learnable visual center mechanism focuses on key local 
regions to improve feature representation. The model employs 
a top-­down global regulation mechanism, where deep features 
refine shallow ones for better tracking, and a template update 
module adapts reference images to maintain accuracy over 
time. For evaluation, the model was trained and tested using 
the CLUST dataset. The tracking error resulted in an average 
error of 0.79 mm, a maximum error of 1.92 mm, and a standard 
deviation of 0.31 mm. The tracking speed reached 80–105 fps. 
The advantage of this comes from the TACNN module, which 
utilized AlexNet as the backbone network. This method excels 
in high tracking accuracy, real-­time performance, and adapt-
ability to dynamic motion, making it suitable for clinical appli-
cations. However, it may require high computational resources 
and fine-­tuning.

3.1.3   |   Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
GANs consist of two competing models: a generator (G) that 
creates synthetic data to fool a discriminator (D), which learns 
to distinguish between real and generated data. GAN was used 
in [48] to track US images by estimating how tissue deforms 
over time. The process begins with a sequence of US frames 
(one tracked frame followed by untracked frames). A Markov-­
like network (Figure 5), which behaves similarly to a traditional 
Markov model by relying only on the current state, is used to ex-
tract features from these frames. In GAN network, the genera-
tor predicts deformation vector fields (DVFs) representing tissue 
motion between frames, while the discriminator distinguishes 
between real US images and those spatially transformed using 
the estimated DVFs. Through adversarial training, the network 
improves motion estimation accuracy. Landmark positions in 
untracked frames are then inferred by shifting them according 
to the estimated DVFs from tracked frames [48]. The method 
was tested on 2D US sequences of CLUST. The results showed 
accuracy with a mean tracking error of 0.70 ± 0.38 mm.
3.1.4   |   Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs)
Long-­term US tracking requires temporal modeling due to 
changes in target and background appearance. RNNs address 
this by capturing motion patterns over time, making them more 
suitable than CNNs for tracking dynamic sequences. Long 
Short-­Term Memory (LSTM) networks are a type of RNN de-
signed to capture long-­term dependencies by using the memory 
cell, regulated by input, forget, and output gates, which control 
information flow and prevent vanishing gradients, enabling ef-
fective temporal learning.
The LSTM has been used in [28] to predict the heat map of the 
specific landmark for the next frame. The features were ex-
tracted from the past three frames using CNN. The RNN uses 
the CNN encoder and decoder to generate tracking predictions 
from the input sequence. This tracker achieved a mean error of 
0.51 ± 0.31 mm on the CIL-­01 sequence of CLUST to train the 
model and tested on the rest of the sequence. However, the data-
set size was limited for robust validation.
In [29] an extension of attention-­aware fully connected LSTM 
which has convolutional structures in both the input-­to-­
state and state-­to-­state transitions were proposed (Figure  6). 
Convolutional LSTM (ConvLSTM) has potential to model well 
the spatio-­temporal relationships, while the traditional LSTM 
does not take spatial correlation into consideration. The atten-
tion mechanism focuses on the region of interest while dis-
carding irrelevant background, allowing the FCNN to extract 
spatial features that are then processed by the ConvLSTM for 
temporal modeling. A saliency mask further refines the tracked 
landmarks, enhancing accuracy. To improve training stability 
and prevent overfitting, a multitask loss strategy was employed.

The cascade DL model proposed in [49] combines an attention

3.1.5   |   Hybrid Approaches in 2D Tracking: Combining 
DL and Conventional Techniques
Hybrid methods that integrate conventional tracking techniques 
with DL are gaining attention in US tracking due to their com-
plementary strengths. Classical methods, such as optical flow, 
correlation-­based tracking, and Kalman filtering, offer interpre-
table motion models and do not require large annotated datasets. 
While classical tracking methods require no training and can be 
directly applied to new data, they often involve higher compu-
tational complexity during inference, especially in 3D or long 
sequences. On the other hand, DL models can learn complex 
representations and adapt to diverse imaging conditions, but 
are often limited by their need for labeled data. DL approaches 
demand substantial resources during training but can offer fast 
inference times when deployed on optimized hardware, making 
them increasingly attractive for real-­time applications. Hybrid 
approaches aim to bridge this gap. In [43], a conventional filter 
(Kalman filter) is used to guide or correct the output of DL mod-
els, and [50] uses classical tracking to generate pseudo-­labels or 
to identify challenging frames with occlusion or out-­of-­screen 
artifacts, where DL is selectively applied.
In [51], the SiamFC architecture [43] was upgraded to address 
limitations related to deformation sensitivity and the lack of a 
motion model. To overcome these two limitations, a template 
update module was added to handle object deformations, and 
a kalman filter linear motion model was incorporated. The 
Kalman filter predicted the centroid of the reference block, 
which was then corrected using SiamFC's matching result. If 
the corrected output met a correlation threshold, the reference 
was updated; otherwise, a previous reliable frame was restored. 
This helped mitigate tracking drift and deformation sensitivity. 
The proposed model (Figure 7a) was evaluated on 2D US images 
of CLUST dataset with overall accuracy of 1.59 ± 3.68 mm.
Another notable example is the EKLT (Enhanced Kanade–
Lucas–Tomasi)-­LSTM method [50], which combines traditional 
tracking using Enhanced KLT with an LSTM network. This 
EKLT framework incorporates an internal measurement unit 
that assesses the visibility of the ROI and detects significant 
drops in tracking accuracy. In challenging scenarios, such as 
occlusions, out-­of-­screen motion, or high image noise, a trained 
LSTM module is activated to maintain tracking performance 
over short intervals. This work is the first to propose the use of 
DL to specifically address occlusion in US tracking and allows 
for adaptive switching between methods depending on tracking 
confidence. The proposed network (Figure 7b) was evaluated on

3.2   |   3D US Tracking
3D US tracking estimates volumetric motion and provides depth 
information that is essential for accurately capturing complex 
anatomical deformations. Compared to 2D tracking, it offers 
improved robustness to out-­of-­plane motion and enables more 
comprehensive spatial context. However, it introduces chal-
lenges related to lower frame rates, increased data storage and 
processing requirements, and reduced spatial resolution due to 
slice reconstruction. In this section, we organize 3D tracking 
methods based on their primary architecture.
3.2.1   |   CNNs
Inspired by conventional speckle tracking, one of the early DL 
approaches extracted and aggregated local features to estimate 
motion vectors. Building on this idea, Reference [27] proposed 
a Deep Contextual Learning Network (DCL-­Net) for 3D US, 
which leveraged multiple consecutive frames and incorpo-
rated an attention mechanism to focus on speckle-­rich regions, 
thereby improving motion estimation and reconstruction accu-
racy. This approach demonstrated the potential of DL for 3D US 
tracking and encouraged further exploration of volumetric mo-
tion estimation.
3.2.2   |   Siamese Networks
An approach was presented by Huang et al. [52], where a fully 
connected CNN (FCNN) was utilized for 3D US tracking. In 
their design, the FCNN was coupled with scale discriminative 
correlation filter (SDCF) shown in Figure 8a. FCNN is used to 
extract convolutional features, and the extracted features are fed 
to the SDCF to calculate the location probability map. SDCF is 
used as a differentiable layer, which ensures that the network 
performs scale learning and end-­to-­end training. The end-­to-­
end network was trained on millions of 2D natural images with 
RGB three channels in ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition 
Challenge (ILSRVC) 2015 [54] dataset. Then, the 3D US image 
is transformed into a 2D three-­channel representation. The spa-
tial information of each voxel is represented by three orthogo-
nal plane—axial, sagittal, and coronal-­surrounding the voxel 
of interest. These three planes are then combined into a three-­
channel image, which is used as the input for the network. The 
end-­to-­end network is trained to compute similarities between 
the target and search regions in the US images. In 2D US track-
ing, this is done by locating the pixel with the highest value in a 
probability map, which represents the location of the landmark. 
In contrast, for 3D US, the probability map measures the simi-
larity between the target and candidate landmarks but does not 
directly show the landmarks location. Instead, the maximum 
value in the map indicates the best match between the target 
and a potential candidate landmark. The approach addresses a 
common challenge in tracking methods known as the bound-
ary effect, where outliers near the edges of the image distort 
the tracking results. To mitigate this issue, the paper proposed 
a method to process the probability map, preventing boundary 
artifacts from negatively impacting the tracking. The tracking 
performance was evaluated on the CLUST dataset with 16 sets 
of 3D US landmark sequences in the training dataset and 22 
sets of 3D US landmark sequences in the test dataset, obtain-
ing mean tracking error of 1.63 ± 1.04 mm. The algorithm was 
highly sensitive to short target disappearances, causing it to rely 
heavily on visual information, which resulted in a large maxi-
mum error in such cases. Also, it took this algorithm about 0.3 s 
to process a frame.

patches and two CNN subnetworks are used to extract deep 
features from these patches. The algorithm integrates a Spatial

3.2.3   |   Convolution Auto-­Encoders (CAE)
Autoencoders (AEs) are neural networks that learn efficient data 
representations by compressing input into a low-­dimensional 
space and then reconstructing the original image. A CAE 
achieves this through an encoder, which extracts features using 
convolutional layers, and a decoder, which reconstructs the 
image using transposed convolution (deconvolution) or upsam-
pling layers.
The method in [56] applies a CAE framework to integrate 2D 
and 3D US imaging for real-­time anatomical landmark tracking. 
It infers a 3D volume at time tn by combining a 2D US image at 
tn with a baseline 3D volume at t0. Two fully convolutional CAEs 
extract features from both inputs, which are fused to estimate a 
deformation field applied to the reference volume (Figure 9a). A 
spatial transformer network (STN) refines the transformation, en-
abling non-­rigid alignment. STNs [58] are differentiable modules 
that learn spatial transformations and support end-­to-­end train-
ing. This approach avoids repeated 3D scans and enables real-­time 
3D volume estimation. Trained on 20 3D liver US sequences from 
CLUST, the model achieved a mean landmark tracking error of 
2.92 ± 1.67 mm. Limitations include reduced image resolution and 
limited volume thickness compared to the ground truth.

3.2.4   |   GANs
The suggested Markov-­like GAN network in [48] (Figure 5) was 
also tested on 3D US sequences of CLUST. The results showed 
accuracy with a mean tracking error of 1.71 ± 0.8 mm.
Building on GANs concept, Giger et al. [59] proposed a subject-­
specific respiratory motion model using conditional GANs 
(cGANs). In their approach, cGAN predicts 3D deformations 
based on 2D US images. To enhance accuracy, they introduced 
gradient information by feeding two consecutive US images into 
the cGAN, with the network trained for two input and two out-
put channels to handle deformation fields in both x and y direc-
tions. Additionally, they incorporated a time shift in the training 
process: the cGAN predicts the deformation field at time ti+1 
using US images from times ti−1 and ti−2. The median error of this 
approach was below 1 mm and the maximum error below 3 mm. 
While promising, the method was validated on only three sub-
jects, indicating the need for further testing on larger datasets.

4   |   Discussion
In the previous section, we reviewed methods that utilize DL 
for RIM tracking in 2D and 3D US images. When discussing the 
reviewed methods in the previous section, we highlighted both 
their strengths and limitations. Here, for better comparison, 
Tables 1 and 2 summarize the performance, runtime, architec-
ture, and reported strengths and limitations of each category.
Prior to compare DL methods, various conventional methods 
were developed for US tracking. These include block match-
ing [61], optical flow [20], feature-­based tracking [19], template 
matching [18], and active contour [62] models. While these ap-
proaches have demonstrated notable success, each comes with 
critical limitations. Block-­matching, though intuitive, is sensi-
tive to speckle noise and suffers from high computational de-
mands when dense tracking is required. Feature-­based methods 
often fail in low-­contrast, noisy environments, and optical flow 
techniques can be unstable due to the complex and non-­rigid na-
ture of tissue motion in US. Template matching is hindered by 
anatomical variability and partial occlusion, while active con-
tours require precise initialization and are susceptible to noise 
and shadowing. Comparative evaluations of conventional meth-
ods exist, and previous surveys in this field have predominantly 
focused on benchmarking these traditional approaches. For 
instance, [18] compared multiple algorithms developed for the 
CLUST challenge on 2D and 3D liver sequences, with a fusion-­
based method achieving the best performance (0.92 ± 0.98 mm). 
In 3D tracking, the combination of intensity-­based registration 
and the mechanical model achieved the highest accuracy, with a 
reported overall error of 1.74 ± 0.92 mm in the CLUST challenge. 
To overcome limitations such as out-­of-­plane motion, abrupt 
deformations, speckle noise, occlusion, and low contrast, deep 
learning models have been applied to capture complex motion 
patterns, enhance robustness to artifacts, and improve general-
ization across varying image conditions.
In DL methods, 2D tracking (Table 1) remains the most widely 
explored approach in the reviewed literature, owing to its lower 
computational requirements, widespread availability of 2D US 
systems, and real-­time imaging capability. Methods evaluated 
on the CLUST dataset demonstrate a wide range of performance 
depending on architecture complexity and training strategy. The

These DL-­based approaches demonstrate notable improvements 
in tracking accuracy compared to conventional methods, partic-
ularly in reducing drift and improving robustness to tissue mo-
tion. However, limitations remain, especially in the presence of 
occlusion, out-­of-­screen and abrupt motion, and computational 
inefficiencies in more complex models. To overcome limitations 
of 2D tracking, particularly in handling out-­of-­plane motion 
and image artifacts, hybrid solutions have emerged as promis-
ing alternatives. One category involves combining traditional 
tracking techniques with DL. For example, in [50], KLT is used 
for frame-­to-­frame tracking, while a parallel module evaluates 
frame quality to detect occlusions or noise. In such cases, a 
trained LSTM model takes over, enabling robust tracking under 
challenging conditions. These hybrid model-­level frameworks 
can be further developed to handle a broader range of artifacts 
and dynamic scenarios, offering adaptable and modular track-
ing solutions. Despite their promise, current hybrid methods 
remain underexplored and underdeveloped. A more systematic 
exploration of fusion strategies, such as shared feature spaces, 
weighted decision fusion, or learning-­based confidence estima-
tion, could unlock greater robustness. These strategies are par-
ticularly important for handling challenging clinical scenarios 
like occlusion, deformation, or rapid motion.
A second category of hybrid solutions involves sensor fusion, 
where external signals, such as accelerometers, respiratory belts, 
or impedance-­based sensors, are used to estimate breathing mo-
tion. These signals can be synchronized and integrated with DL 
models to improve tracking robustness, particularly when US 
visibility is limited. While many surrogate sensors have been 
introduced and widely used in other imaging modalities such 
as CT or MRI [63, 64], their integration with US-­based tracking 
remains largely unexplored. This represents a promising direc-
tion for future research, with the potential to enhance motion 
compensation in applications like radiotherapy, where both pre-
cision and adaptability are critical.
In terms of clinical applicability, 2D methods are promising for 
real-­time tracking during in-­plane interventional procedures, 
particularly when the target remains within the imaging plane. 
However, for procedures where targets move significantly out of 
plane, 2D tracking alone may be insufficient. Hybrid solutions 
or integration with external sensors may be needed to maintain 
spatial accuracy.
3D US (Table 2) enables volumetric tracking and provide depth 
information critical for more accurate motion estimation. In 
the CLUST 3D dataset, the methods [48, 52] show similar accu-
racy, with errors of 1.63 ± 1.04 and 1.71 ± 0.84 mm, respectively. 
Reference [48] stands out because it performs well on both 2D 
and 3D images.
The methods for the Ipsen dataset focus on 3D US tracking. 
Among these, the most recent approach, [39], which uses a de-
formable AE, achieves the best performance with an error of 
1.58 ± 0.87 mm and a fast runtime of 4 ms per frame.
3D tracking involves estimating motion within volumetric data, 
which requires processing spatial information across all three 
dimensions. This introduces additional challenges and steps. 3D 
data acquisition often involves mechanical sweeping or matrix 
array probes, which can result in varying volume quality and 
lower temporal resolution. In addition, data preprocessing such 
as slice interpolation, normalization of voxel sizes, and sub-­
volume extraction becomes essential. Models must be adapted to 
handle volumetric inputs, commonly through 3D convolutional 
networks, patch-­based methods, or encoder–decoder architec-
tures with latent representation learning. Additionally, 3D mod-
els often require more computational resources and may need 
architectural modifications or GPU optimization to maintain 
acceptable run times. Thus, 3D tracking remains constrained 
by lower frame rates, high computational load, and memory re-
quirements. To address these, future work should focus on de-
veloping lightweight architectures, efficient temporal modeling, 
and domain-­adaptive learning strategies that perform robustly 
across diverse imaging conditions.
From a clinical perspective, 2D and 3D US tracking methods are 
applicable to different interventional and therapeutic scenarios 
including image-­guided procedures/surgery, IGRT, and end-­
organ US stimulation, each with distinct accuracy and timing 
requirements. In US-­guided procedures such as needle biopsies, 
ablations, and regional anesthesia, 2D tracking is commonly 
used due to its real-­time display and satisfactory spatial preci-
sion as long as the target remains in-­plane. Such applications 
demand frame rates around 18–30 fps to allow continuous vi-
sualization and precise tool guidance [65]. Several reviewed 2D 
tracking models in this paper demonstrate sub-­millimeter accu-
racy and runtimes below 33 ms per frame, which are well suited 
to meet the demands of these real-­time clinical applications. 
Procedures like IGRT require tracking of complex respiratory-­
induced 3D tumor motion. While some setups permit simpli-
fied 2D tracking in planes perpendicular to the beam direction, 
many treatment workflows benefit from full 3D tracking to ac-
count for out-­of-­plane displacement. The reviewed 3D methods, 
such as [48, 52], report average errors around 1.6–1.7 mm, meet-
ing the spatial precision requirements for radiation therapy, 
which typically demand accuracy within 2 mm outlined by the 
AAPM Task Group [66]. Although the frame rate requirement 
in this setting is more relaxed (often 5–15 fps), the system must 
maintain a total latency of no more than approximately 0.5 s, as 
motion prediction becomes unreliable beyond this range and the 
benefit of real-­time tracking diminishes [66]. In conventional 
motion tracking, the integration of temporal prediction has been 
shown to be critical for compensating system latency in IGRT

Several existing US tracking models demonstrate low latency

integration, they could meet the performance requirements for 
real-­time use. However, despite promising results, most DL-­

and are not yet clinically deployed. Several key challenges hin-
der their broader adoption. One major limitation is the difficulty 
in collecting large, diverse, and well-­annotated datasets due 
to the high costs of clinical data acquisition and expert label-
ing. This highlights the need for data-­efficient DL algorithms. 
Another important challenge is data mismatch, when models 
trained under specific conditions fail to generalize to real-­world 
clinical settings. Variability in US images caused by differences 
in operators, patients, or US devices further impacts model ro-
bustness. Although recent studies [67, 68] have explored trans-
fer function-­based techniques and domain adaptation strategies 
[69] to improve cross-­device generalizability, these efforts re-
main limited in scope and are mostly demonstrated on phan-
tom data. Future work should explore these strategies more 
thoroughly using larger and more diverse clinical datasets to en-
sure reliable performance in real-­world applications. Therefore, 
addressing these gaps by curating multi-­device datasets, apply-
ing domain adaptation or transfer learning techniques, and ex-
ploring device-­agnostic network architectures or pre-­processing 
pipelines to enhance generalization is another future direction.
5   |   Conclusion
US offers several advantages over other imaging modalities, in-
cluding safety, portability, cost-­effectiveness, high temporal res-
olution, and real-­time capability. As a result, there is a growing 
trend to integrate automation into US-­guided therapies. To this 
end, several DL architectures have recently been proposed to en-
able end-­to-­end tracking and prediction models. In this work, we

Abstract: Ultrasound (US) imaging is widely used in image-­guided therapies due to its real-­time capability, high temporal resolution, cost-­ effectiveness, safety, and portability. While many US tracking methods exist, most reviews focus on conventional techniques and overlook recent advances in deep learning (DL). Existing DL surveys often emphasize modalities like MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) or CT (Computed Tomography), but US tracking presents unique challenges, such as speckle noise, acoustic shadow- ing, and occlusions, that require tailored solutions. With increasing interest in automating US-­guided procedures, particularly for respiratory-­induced motion (RIM) tracking, this review fills a gap by focusing on recent DL-­based methods specifically developed for US motion tracking. We conducted a targeted review of state-­of-­the-­art DL techniques, categorizing them by net- work architecture. Special attention is given to studies using benchmark datasets like CLUST (Challenge on Liver Ultrasound Tracking), which enable standardized performance comparison. DL-­based methods demonstrate improved accuracy and robust- ness in difficult scenarios, such as out-­of-­plane motion and occlusions, where traditional approaches often underperform. DL has significantly improved the feasibility of markerless US tracking in clinical settings, supporting more automated and reliable image-­guided interventions. While conventional methods still offer value, hybrid strategies that integrate DL with traditional tracking or sensor fusion approaches show strong potential. This review complements prior surveys on conventional US tracking, serving as a useful resource for researchers developing robust, automated US-­based applications.
